And what if I should assume, then, that the man to whom we ought all to listen is he who has this capacity of judgement and who has lived under the same roof with a tyrant and has witnessed his conduct in his own home and observed in person {577b} his dealings with his intimates in each instance where he would best be seen stripped of his vesture of tragedy, and who had likewise observed his behavior in the hazards of his public life—and if we should ask the man who has seen all this to be the messenger to report on the happiness or misery of the tyrant as compared with other men? {/q} {q} That also would be a most just challenge, {/q} he said. {q} Shall we, then, make believe, {/q} said I, {q} that we are of those who are thus able to judge and who have ere now lived with tyrants, so that we may have someone to answer our questions? {/q} {q} By all means. {/q} {577c} {p} {q} Come, then, {/q} said I, {q} examine it thus. Recall the general likeness between the city and the man, and then observe in turn what happens to each of them. {/q} {q} What things? {/q} he said. {q} In the first place, {/q} said I, {q} will you call the state governed by a tyrant free or enslaved, speaking of it as a state? {/q} {q} Utterly enslaved, {/q} he said. {q} And yet you see in it masters and freemen. {/q} {q} I see, {/q} he said, {q} a small portion of such, but the entirety, so to speak, and the best part of it, is shamefully and wretchedly enslaved. {/q} {q} If, then, {/q} I said, {577d} {q} the man resembles the state, must not the same proportion obtain in him, and his soul teem with boundless servility and illiberality, the best and most reasonable parts of it being enslaved, while a small part, the worst and the most frenzied, plays the despot? {/q} {q} Inevitably, {/q} he said. {q} Then will you say that such a soul is enslaved or free? {/q} {q} Enslaved, I should suppose. {/q} {q} Again, does not the enslaved and tyrannized city least of all do what it really wishes? {/q} {q} Decidedly so. {/q} {q} Then the tyrannized soul— {577e} to speak of the soul as a whole—also will least of all do what it wishes, but being always perforce driven and drawn by the gadfly of desire it will be full of confusion and repentance. {/q} {q} Of course. {/q} {q} And must the tyrannized city {578a} be rich or poor? {/q} {q} Poor. {/q}
{q} Then the tyrant soul also must of necessity always be needy and suffer from unfulfilled desire. {/q} {q} So it is, {/q} he said. {q} And again, must not such a city, as well as such a man, be full of terrors and alarms? {/q} {q} It must indeed. {/q} {q} And do you think you will find more lamentations and groans and wailing and anguish in any other city? {/q} {q} By no means. {/q} {q} And so of man, do you think these things will more abound in any other than in this tyrant type, that is maddened by its desires and passions? {/q} {q} How could it be so? {/q} he said. {q} In view of all these {578b} and other like considerations, then, I take it, you judged that this city is the most miserable of cities. {/q} {q} And was I not right? {/q} he said. {q} Yes, indeed, {/q} said I. {q} But of the tyrant man, what have you to say in view of these same things? {/q} {q} That he is far and away the most miserable of all, {/q} he said. {q} I cannot admit, {/q} said I, {q} that you are right in that too. {/q} {q} How so? {/q} said he. {q} This one, {/q} said I, {q} I take it, has not yet attained the acme of misery. {/q} {q} Then who has? {/q} {q} Perhaps you will regard the one I am about to name as still more wretched. {/q} {578c} {q} What one? {/q} {q} The one, {/q} said I, {q} who, being of tyrannical temper, does not live out his life in private station but is so unfortunate that by some unhappy chance he is enabled to become an actual tyrant. {/q} {q} I infer from what has already been said, {/q} he replied, {q} that you speak truly. {/q} {q} Yes, {/q} said I, {q} but it is not enough to suppose such things. We must examine them thoroughly by reason and an argument such as this. For our inquiry concerns the greatest of all things, the good life or the bad life. {/q} {q} Quite right, {/q} he replied. {q} Consider, then, if there is anything in what I say. {578d} For I think we must get a notion of the matter from these examples. {/q} {q} From which? {/q} {q} From individual wealthy private citizens in our states who possess many slaves. For these resemble the tyrant in being rulers over many, only the tyrant’s numbers are greater. {/q} {q} Yes, they are. {/q} {q} You are aware, then, that they are unafraid and do not fear their slaves? {/q} {q} What should they fear? {/q} {q} Nothing, {/q} I said; {q} but do you perceive the reason why? {/q} {q} Yes, because the entire state {578e} is ready to defend each citizen. {/q} {q} You are right, {/q} I said. {q} But now suppose some god should catch up a man who has fifty or more slaves and waft him with his wife and children away from the city and set him down with his other possessions and his slaves in a solitude where no freeman could come to his rescue. What and how great would be his fear, do you suppose, lest he and his wife and children be destroyed by the slaves? {/q} {q} The greatest in the world, {/q} he said, {q} if you ask me. {/q}
{579a} {q} And would he not forthwith find it necessary to fawn upon some of the slaves and make them many promises and emancipate them, though nothing would be further from his wish? And so he would turn out to be the flatterer of his own servants. {/q} {q} He would certainly have to, {/q} he said, {q} or else perish. {/q} {q} But now suppose, {/q} said I, {q} that god established round about him numerous neighbors who would not tolerate the claim of one man to be master of another, but would inflict the utmost penalties on any such person on whom they could lay their hands. {/q} {q} I think, {/q} he said, {579b} {q} that his plight would be still more desperate, encompassed by nothing but enemies. {/q} {q} And is not that the sort of prison-house in which the tyrant is pent, being of a nature such as we have described and filled with multitudinous and manifold terrors and appetites? Yet greedy and avid of spirit as he is, he only of the citizens may not travel abroad or view any of the sacred festivals that other freemen yearn to see, but he must live for the most part cowering in the recesses of his house like a woman, {579c} envying among the other citizens anyone who goes abroad and sees any good thing. {/q} {q} Most certainly, {/q} he said. {p} {q} And does not such a harvest of ills measure the difference between the man who is merely ill-governed in his own soul, the man of tyrannical temper, whom you just now judged to be most miserable, and the man who, having this disposition, does not live out his life in private station but is constrained by some ill hap to become an actual tyrant, and while unable to control himself attempts to rule over others, as if a man with a sick and incontinent body should not live the private life but should be compelled {579d} to pass his days in contention and strife with other persons? {/q} {q} Your analogy is most apt and true, Socrates, {/q} he said. {q} Is not that then, dear Glaucon, {/q} said I, {q} a most unhappy experience in every way? And is not the tyrant’s life still worse than that which was judged by you to be the worst? {/q} {q} Precisely so, {/q} he said. {q} Then it is the truth, though some may deny it, that the real tyrant is really enslaved {579e} to cringings and servitudes beyond compare, a flatterer of the basest men, and that, so far from finding even the least satisfaction for his desires, he is in need of most things, and is a poor man in very truth, as is apparent if one knows how to observe a soul in its entirety; and throughout his life he teems with terrors and is full of convulsions and pains, if in fact he resembles the condition of the city which he rules; and he is like it, is he not? {/q} {580a} {q} Yes, indeed, {/q} he said.
{q} And in addition, shall we not further attribute to him all that we spoke of before, and say that he must needs be, and, by reason of his rule, come to be still more than he was, envious, faithless, unjust, friendless, impious, a vessel and nurse of all iniquity, and so in consequence be himself most unhappy make all about him so? {/q} {q} No man of sense will gainsay that, {/q} he said. {q} Come then, {/q} said I, {580b} {q} now at last, even as the judge of last instance pronounces, so do you declare who in your opinion is first in happiness and who second, and similarly judge the others, all five in succession, the royal, the timocratic, the oligarchic, the democratic, and the tyrannical man. {/q} {q} Nay, {/q} he said, {q} the decision is easy. For as if they were choruses I judge them in the order of their entrance, and so rank them in respect of virtue and vice, happiness and its contrary. {/q} {q} Shall we hire a herald, then, {/q} said I, {q} or shall I myself make proclamation that the son of Ariston pronounced the best man and the most righteous to be the happiest, {580c} and that he is the one who is the most kingly and a king over himself; and declared that the most evil and most unjust is the most unhappy, who again is the man who, having the most of the tyrannical temper in himself, become, most of a tyrant over himself and over the state? {/q} {q} Let it have been so proclaimed by you, {/q} he said. {q} Shall I add the clause {q} alike whether their character is known to all men and gods or is not known {/q} ? {/q} {q} Add that to the proclamation, {/q} he said. {p} {q} Very good, {/q} said I; {q} this, then, would be one of our proofs, {580d} but examine this second one and see if there is anything in it. {/q} {q} What is it? {/q} {q} Since, {/q} said I, {q} corresponding to the three types in the city, the soul also is tripartite, it will admit, I think, of another demonstration also. {/q} {q} What is that? {/q} {q} The following: The three parts have also, it appears to me, three kinds of pleasure, one peculiar to each, and similarly three appetites and controls. {/q} {q} What do you mean? {/q} he said. {q} One part, we say, is that with which a man learns, one is that with which he feels anger. But the third part, owing to its manifold forms, we could not easily designate by any one distinctive name, {580e} but gave it the name of its chief and strongest element; {/q}
{q} for we called it the appetitive part because of the intensity of its appetites concerned with food and drink and love and their accompaniments, and likewise the money-loving part, because money is the chief instrument {581a} for the gratification of such desires. {/q} {q} And rightly, {/q} he said. {q} And if we should also say that its pleasure and its love were for gain or profit, should we not thus best bring it together under one head in our discourse so as to understand each other when we speak of this part of the soul, and justify our calling it the money-loving and gain-loving part? {/q} {q} I, at any rate, think so, {/q} he said. {q} And, again, of the high-spirited element, do we not say that it is wholly set on predominance and victory and good repute? {/q} {581b} {q} Yes, indeed. {/q} {q} And might we not appropriately designate it as the ambitious part and that which is covetous of honor? {/q} {q} Most appropriately. {/q} {q} But surely it is obvious to everyone that all the endeavor of the part by which we learn is ever towards knowledge of the truth of things, and that it least of the three is concerned for wealth and reputation. {/q} {q} Much the least. {/q} {q} Lover of learning and lover of wisdom would be suitable designations for that. {/q} {q} Quite so, {/q} he said. {q} Is it not also true, {/q} I said, {581c} {q} that the ruling principle of men’s souls is in some cases this faculty and in others one of the other two, as it may happen? {/q} {q} That is so, {/q} he said. {q} And that is why we say that the primary classes of men also are three, the philosopher or lover of wisdom, the lover of victory and the lover of gain. {/q} {q} Precisely so {/q} {q} And also that there are three forms of pleasure, corresponding respectively to each? {/q} {q} By all means. {/q} {q} Are you aware, then {/q} said I, {q} that if you should choose to ask men of these three classes, each in turn, which is the most pleasurable of these lives, each will chiefly commend his own? The financier {581d} will affirm that in comparison with profit the pleasures of honor or of learning area of no value except in so far as they produce money. {/q} {q} True, {/q} he said. {q} And what of the lover of honor? {/q} I said; {q} does he not regard the pleasure that comes from money as vulgar and low, and again that of learning, save in so far as the knowledge confers honor, mere fume and moonshine? {/q} {q} It is so, {/q} he said. {q} And what, {/q} said I, {q} are we to suppose the philosopher thinks of the other pleasures {581e} compared with the delight of knowing the truth and the reality, and being always occupied with that while he learns? Will he not think them far removed from true pleasure, and call them literally the pleasures of necessity, since he would have no use for them if necessity were not laid upon him? {/q}
{q} We may be sure of that, {/q} he said. {p} {q} Since, then, there is contention between the several types of pleasure and the lives themselves, not merely as to which is the more honorable or the more base, or the worse or the better, but which is actually the more pleasurable or free from pain, {582a} how could we determine which of them speaks most truly? {/q} {q} In faith, I cannot tell, {/q} he said. {q} Well, consider it thus: By what are things to be judged, if they are to be judged rightly? Is it not by experience, intelligence and discussion? Or could anyone name a better criterion than these? {/q} {q} How could he? {/q} he said. {q} Observe, then. Of our three types of men, which has had the most experience of all the pleasures we mentioned? Is he more unacquainted with the pleasure of being honored than that other with that which comes from knowledge? {/q} {q} Nay, honor, {/q} he said, {q} if they achieve their several objects, attends them all; for the rich man is honored by many and the brave man and the wise, so that all are acquainted with the kind of pleasure that honor brings; but it is impossible for anyone except the lover of wisdom to have savored the delight that the contemplation of true being and reality brings. {/q} {582d} {q} Then, {/q} said I, {q} so far as experience goes, he is the best judge of the three. {/q} {q} By far. {/q} {q} And again, he is the only one whose experience will have been accompanied by intelligence. {/q} {q} Surely. {/q} {q} And yet again, that which is the instrument, or ὄργανον, of judgement is the instrument, not of the lover of gain or of the lover of honor, but of the lover of wisdom. {/q} {q} What is that? {/q} {q} It was by means of words and discussion that we said the judgement must be reached; was it not? {/q} {q} Yes. {/q} {q} And they are the instrument mainly of the philosopher. {/q} {q} Of course. {/q} {q} Now if wealth and profit were the best criteria by which things are judged, {582e} the things praised and censured by the lover of gain would necessarily be truest and most real. {/q} {q} Quite necessarily. {/q} {q} And if honor, victory and courage, would it not be the things praised by the lover of honor and victory? {/q} {q} Obviously. {/q} {q} But since the tests are experience and wisdom and discussion, what follows? {/q} {q} Of necessity, {/q} he said, {q} that the things approved by the lover of wisdom and discussion are most valid and true. {/q}
{583a} {q} There being, then, three kinds of pleasure, the pleasure of that part of the soul whereby we learn is the sweetest, and the life of the man in whom that part dominates is the most pleasurable. {/q} {q} How could it be otherwise? {/q} he said. {q} At any rate the man of intelligence speaks with authority when he commends his own life. {/q} {q} And to what life and to what pleasure, {/q} I said, {q} does the judge assign the second place? {/q} {q} Obviously to that of the warrior and honor-loving type, for it is nearer to the first than is the life of the money-maker. {/q} {q} And so the last place belongs to the lover of gain, as it seems. {/q} {q} Surely, {/q} said he. {583b} {p} {q} That, then, would be two points in succession and two victories for the just man over the unjust. And now for the third in the Olympian fashion to the saviour and to Olympian Zeus—observe that other pleasure than that of the intelligence is not altogether even real or pure, but is a kind of scene-painting, as I seem to have heard from some wise man; and yet this would be the greatest and most decisive overthrow. {/q} {q} Much the greatest. But what do you mean? {/q} {q} I shall discover it, {/q} I said, {583c} {q} if you will answer my questions while I seek. {/q} {q} Ask, then, {/q} he said. {q} Tell me, then, {/q} said I, {q} do we not say that pain is the opposite of pleasure? {/q} {q} We certainly do. {/q} {q} And is there not such a thing as a neutral state {/q} {q} There is. {/q} {q} Is it not intermediate between them, and in the mean, being a kind of quietude of the soul in these respects? Or is not that your notion of it? {/q} {q} It is that, {/q} said he. {q} Do you not recall the things men say in sickness? {/q} {q} What sort of things? {/q} {q} Why, that after all there is nothing sweeter than to be well, {583d} though they were not aware that it is the highest pleasure before they were Ill. {/q} {q} I remember, {/q} he said. {q} And do you not hear men afflicted with severe pain saying that there is no greater pleasure than the cessation of this suffering? {/q} {q} I do. {/q} {q} And you perceive, I presume, many similar conditions in which men while suffering pain praise freedom from pain and relief from that as the highest pleasure, and not positive delight. {/q} {q} Yes, {/q} he said, {q} for this in such cases is perhaps what is felt as pleasurable and acceptable—peace. {/q} {583e} {q} And so, {/q} I said, {q} when a man’s delight comes to an end, the cessation of pleasure will be painful. {/q} {q} It may be so, {/q} he said. {q} What, then,we just now described as the intermediate state between the two—this quietude—will sometimes be both pain and pleasure. {/q} {q} It seems so {/q} {q} Is it really possible for that which is neither to become both? {/q} {q} I think not. {/q} {q} And further, both pleasure and pain arising in the soul are a kind of motion, are they not? {/q} {584a} {q} Yes. {/q}
{q} And did we not just now see that to feel neither pain nor pleasure is a quietude of the soul and an intermediate state between the two? {/q} {q} Yes, we did. {/q} {q} How, then, can it be right to think the absence of pain pleasure, or the absence of joy painful? {/q} {q} In no way. {/q} {q} This is not a reality, then, but an illusion, {/q} said I; {q} in such case the quietude in juxtaposition with the pain appears pleasure, and in juxtaposition with the pleasure pain. And these illusions have no real bearing on the truth of pleasure, but are a kind of jugglery. {/q} {q} So at any rate our argument signifies, {/q} he said. {q} Take a look, then, {/q} {584b} said I, {q} at pleasures which do not follow on pain, so that you may not haply suppose for the present that it is the nature of pleasure to be a cessation from pain and pain from pleasure. {/q} {q} Where shall I look, {/q} he said, {q} and what pleasures do you mean? {/q} {q} There are many others, {/q} I said, {q} and especially, if you please to note them, the pleasures connected with smell. For these with no antecedent pain suddenly attain an indescribable intensity, and their cessation leaves no pain after them. {/q} {q} Most true, {/q} he said. {q} Let us not believe, then, {584c} that the riddance of pain is pure pleasure or that of pleasure pain. {/q} {q} No, we must not. {/q} {q} Yet, surely, {/q} said I, {q} the affections that find their way through the body to the soul and are called pleasures are, we may say, the most and the greatest of them, of this type, in some sort releases from pain.? {/q} {q} Yes, they are. {/q} {q} And is not this also the character of the anticipatory pleasures and pains that precede them and arise from the expectation of them? {/q} {q} It is. {/q} {584d} {p} {q} Do you know, then, what their quality is and what they most resemble? {/q} {q} What? {/q} he said. {q} Do you think that there is such a thing in nature as up and down and in the middle? {/q} {q} I do. {/q} {q} Do you suppose, then, that anyone who is transported from below to the center would have any other opinion than that he was moving upward? And if he took his stand at the center and looked in the direction from which he had been transported, do you think he would suppose himself to be anywhere but above, never having seen that which is really above? {/q} {q} No, by Zeus, {/q} he said, {q} I do not think that such a person would have any other notion. {/q} {584e} {q} And if he were borne back, {/q} I said, {q} he would both think himself to be moving downward and would think truly. {/q} {q} Of course. {/q} {q} And would not all this happen to him because of his non-acquaintance with the true and real up and down and middle? {/q} {q} Obviously. {/q}
{q} Would it surprise you, then, {/q} said I, {q} if similarly men without experience of truth and reality hold unsound opinions about many other matters, and are so disposed towards pleasure and pain and the intermediate neutral condition that, when they are moved in the direction of the painful, {585a} they truly think themselves to be, and really are, in a state of pain, but, when they move from pain to the middle and neutral state, they intensely believe that they are approaching fulfillment and pleasure, and just as if, in ignorance of white, they were comparing grey with black, so, being inexperienced in true pleasure, they are deceived by viewing painlessness in its relation to pain? {/q} {q} No, by Zeus, {/q} he said, {q} it would not surprise me, but far rather if it were not so. {/q} {q} In this way, then, consider it. Are not hunger and thirst and similar states inanitions or emptinesses {585b} of the bodily habit? {/q} {q} Surely. {/q} {q} And is not ignorance and folly in turn a kind of emptiness of the habit of the soul? {/q} {q} It is indeed. {/q} {q} And he who partakes of nourishment and he who gets, wisdom fills the void and is filled? {/q} {q} Of course. {/q} {q} And which is the truer filling and fulfillment, that of the less or of the more real being? {/q} {q} Evidently that of the more real. {/q} {q} And which of the two groups or kinds do you think has a greater part in pure essence, the class of foods, drinks, and relishes and nourishment generally, or the kind of true opinion, {585c} knowledge and reason, and, in sum, all the things that are more excellent? Form your judgement thus. Which do you think more truly is, that which clings to what is ever like itself and immortal and to the truth, and that which is itself of such a nature and is born in a thing of that nature, or that which clings to what is mortal and never the same and is itself such and is born in such a thing? {/q} {q} That which cleaves to what is ever the same far surpasses, {/q} he said. {q} Does the essence of that which never abides the same partake of real essence any more than of knowledge? {/q} {q} By no means. {/q} {q} Or of truth and reality? {/q} {q} Not of that, either. {/q} {q} And if a thing has less of truth has it not also less of real essence or existence? {/q} {q} Necessarily. {/q} {q} And is it not generally true {585d} that the kinds concerned with the service of the body partake less of truth and reality than those that serve the soul? {/q} {q} Much less. {/q} {q} And do you not think that the same holds of the body itself in comparison with the soul? {/q} {q} I do. {/q} {q} Then is not that which is fulfilled of what more truly is, and which itself more truly is, more truly filled and satisfied than that which being itself less real is filled with more unreal things? {/q} {q} Of course. {/q} {q} If, then, to be filled with what befits nature is pleasure, then that which is more really filled with real things {585e} would more really and truly cause us to enjoy a true pleasure, while that which partakes of the less truly existent would be less truly and surely filled and would partake of a less trustworthy and less true pleasure. {/q} {q} Most inevitably, {/q} he said.
{q} Then those who have no experience {586a} of wisdom and virtue but are ever devoted to feastings and that sort of thing are swept downward, it seems, and back again to the center, and so sway and roam to and fro throughout their lives, but they have never transcended all this and turned their eyes to the true upper region nor been wafted there, nor ever been really filled with real things, nor ever tasted stable and pure pleasure, but with eyes ever bent upon the earth and heads bowed down over their tables they feast like cattle, {586b} grazing and copulating, ever greedy for more of these delights; and in their greed kicking and butting one another with horns and hooves of iron they slay one another in sateless avidity, because they are vainly striving to satisfy with things that are not real the unreal and incontinent part of their souls. {/q} {q} You describe in quite oracular style, Socrates, {/q} said Glaucon, {q} the life of the multitude. {/q} {q} And are not the pleasures with which they dwell inevitably commingled with pains, phantoms of true pleasure, illusions of scene-painting, so colored by contrary juxtaposition {586c} as to seem intense in either kind, and to beget mad loves of themselves in senseless souls, and to be fought for, as Stesichorus says the wraith of Helen was fought for at Troy through ignorance of the truth?
